# Quarto and Python {#sec-python}

When you include Python code cells in your document, Quarto uses the Jupyter engine to execute them.
The basics of code cells, including syntax and common options like `echo` and `include`, are covered in @sec-code.
This chapter covers the features specific to Python and Jupyter.

@sec-code-cell-results-python walks through the most common kinds of results Python code cells produce (a single value, a data frame, and a plot), and the options you are most likely to reach for with each.

You'll then see how parameters let one document produce many variations of a report (@sec-parameters-python).
The rest of the chapter, starting with @sec-execution-options-python, covers the details of controlling Python code cells.

::: callout-note

## Code cell fences in this chapter

Remember from @sec-code that code cells are fenced with three backticks and then the engine name in curly braces.
For example, Python code cells look like the following in a Quarto markdown (`.qmd`) file:

```{python}
#| echo: fenced
# Python code goes here
```

:::

In this chapter we omit the fences around code cells in most of the examples, except for those where we want to also display and introduce the code cell options.

Additionally, the examples in this chapter use four Python packages: [**palmerpenguins**](https://github.com/mcnakhaee/palmerpenguins) for data, [**polars**](https://pola.rs/) for working with data frames, [**plotnine**](https://plotnine.org/) for plots, and [**great_tables**](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/) for tables.
Let's import them first:

```{python}
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins
from plotnine import aes, geom_point, ggplot, theme

penguins = pl.from_pandas(load_penguins())
```

`load_penguins()` returns a pandas data frame, so `pl.from_pandas()` converts it to a polars data frame.

When you render, Quarto starts a fresh Jupyter kernel to run this code, not the Python session you might have open in your editor, so the packages need to be installed in the Python environment Quarto uses.

::: callout-tip

## Module not found when rendering?

If Quarto reports `ModuleNotFoundError` even though the import works fine in your Python Console, Quarto is probably running a different Python installation or virtual environment.
See @sec-python-environment for how to diagnose and fix this.

If you render from Positron or VS Code, check that the interpreter selected in your editor is the one with your packages installed.
If you render from a Terminal, make sure the virtual environment with your packages is activated in that Terminal before you run `quarto render`.

:::

TO DO: Installing Quarto CLI with pip, uv pip install is a thing?

## Code cell results {#sec-code-cell-results-python}

### A single value

Start with a code cell that computes a single number: the average body mass of the penguins in the **palmerpenguins** package.
Quarto shows the code followed by its result, as it would appear in a Jupyter notebook:

::: {.rendered}

```{python}
penguins["body_mass_g"].mean()
```

:::

If a code cell produces multiple values, Jupyter displays the value of the last expression, e.g.,:

::: {.rendered}

```{python}
penguins["body_mass_g"].mean()
penguins["body_mass_g"].median()
```

:::

Output like this is fine for showing your work, but if a number belongs in a sentence, you don't want to copy it out of the output by hand.
Instead, save the result in a code cell and insert it into your text with inline code (@sec-inline-code):

```{python}
avg_mass = penguins["body_mass_g"].mean()
```

```markdown
The average penguin weighs `{{python}} round(avg_mass)` grams.
```

This renders as:

> The average penguin weighs `{python} round(avg_mass)` grams.

Because the value is computed every time you render, the sentence stays correct when the data change.

Sometimes you want Python to write more than a single value into your text, for example a bulleted list with one item per species.
Print the markdown with `print()` and set `output: asis`, so that Quarto treats the result as markdown rather than code output:

::: {.rendered}

```{python}
#| echo: fenced
#| output: asis
counts = penguins["species"].value_counts().sort("species")
for species, n in counts.iter_rows():
    print(f"- {species}: {n} penguins")
```

:::

@sec-raw-markdown-output-python covers this technique in more detail, including generating whole sections in a loop.

### A data frame

Data frames are the most common result in a data analysis.
By default, a data frame displays as it would in a Jupyter notebook:

::: {.rendered}

```{python}
penguins
```

:::

Polars shows the shape of the data frame, the type of each column, and the first and last five rows as an HTML table.
In formats that can't display HTML, such as PDF, you get a plain-text version of the same table instead.

<!-- No python counterpart. -->
<!-- The R chapter shows `df-print: paged` here. `df-print` only applies to the knitr engine; see @sec-df-print-python for how to control data frame display with Jupyter. -->

When a table is part of what you're reporting, rather than a quick look at the data, you will want to build it explicitly.
The **great_tables** package turns a data frame into a table you can format and style, and that works in HTML, PDF, and Word output:

::: {.rendered}

```{python}
#| message: false
species_mass = (
    penguins.group_by("species").agg(pl.col("body_mass_g").mean()).sort("species")
)
GT(species_mass).fmt_number(columns="body_mass_g", decimals=0)
```

:::

You can further improve this display by adding a `label` and `tbl-cap` to turn it into a numbered table with a caption that you can cross-reference (@sec-computational-table).
great_tables also has functions for titles, column labels, colors, and much more: the code cell returns a table, and Quarto includes it in your document.

If you want readers to be able to search and sort the data themselves, you can use an interactive table such as `itables.show(penguins)`.
Interactive tables only work in HTML output; @sec-interactive-output-python covers them, along with what to do when you also render to PDF or Word.

### A plot

A code cell that creates a plot includes it in your document as an image:

::: {.rendered}

```{python}
(
    ggplot(penguins, aes(x="flipper_length_mm", y="body_mass_g", color="species"))
    + geom_point()
)
```

:::

If you know ggplot2, plotnine will look familiar: it uses the same grammar of graphics, with column names given as strings and the whole expression wrapped in parentheses so it can span multiple lines.

Two things stand out.
First, plotnine warns about the two penguins with missing measurements.
That warning is useful while you work, but you probably don't want it in your final report.
Second, the plot has no caption, and readers who can't see it get no description of it.
Code cell options take care of both:

::: {.rendered}

```{python}
#| echo: fenced
#| label: fig-mass-flipper
#| fig-cap: Penguins with longer flippers tend to be heavier.
#| fig-alt: Scatterplot of body mass against flipper length for Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins, showing that penguins with longer flippers tend to be heavier.
#| warning: false
(
    ggplot(penguins, aes(x="flipper_length_mm", y="body_mass_g", color="species"))
    + geom_point()
    + theme(figure_size=(6, 4))
)
```

:::

The `fig-` prefix on the label makes the plot a numbered figure you can cross-reference with `@fig-mass-flipper` (@sec-computational-figure).
`fig-alt` adds alternative text and `warning: false` hides the warning.

Unlike with knitr, you can't set the size of a single plot with the `fig-width` and `fig-height` cell options.
Instead, set it in your code; with plotnine, `theme(figure_size=(6, 4))` makes the plot 6 inches wide and 4 inches tall.
You can set `fig-width`, `fig-height`, and `warning` for every cell in the document (@sec-execution-options-python), and plotnine uses those document-level dimensions for any plot that doesn't set its own size.

How a plot looks also depends on the *figure format* Quarto asks matplotlib, which plotnine uses for drawing, to produce.
The defaults work well, but if you want vector output or a different resolution, see @sec-graphics-devices-python.
plotnine plots are static; for plots readers can hover over and zoom into, you need a different plotting library (@sec-interactive-output-python).

## Parameters {#sec-parameters-python}

Every example so far has summarized all the penguins at once.
Suppose you want the same report for each species instead: the same table, plot, and sentences, but for Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins separately.
You could make three copies of the document and edit each one, but then every later change has to be made three times.
Parameters let you write the document once and choose which variation to produce when you render it.

With the Jupyter engine, you define parameters in a code cell, rather than in the YAML header.
Assign each parameter a default value, and add the `parameters` tag so that Quarto knows which cell holds them:

```{{python}}
#| tags: [parameters]
species = "Adelie"
year = 2008
show_details = True
```

This follows the conventions of [Papermill](https://papermill.readthedocs.io/), a tool for parameterizing Jupyter notebooks.
Parameters are ordinary Python variables, so you use them by name in both code cells and inline code:

```{python}
#| eval: false
penguins.filter((pl.col("species") == species) & (pl.col("year") == year))
```

```markdown
This report covers `{{python}} species` penguins observed in `{{python}} year`.
```

Boolean parameters like `show_details` are handy for turning parts of a report on or off.
Jupyter cell options can't be set from Python expressions, so use an `if` statement in the code itself:

```{{python}}
if show_details:
    display(penguins.filter(pl.col("species") == species).describe())
```

`display()` is available in every Jupyter kernel, and is needed here because a value inside an `if` block isn't the last expression in the cell, so Jupyter wouldn't otherwise show it.

You can override the default values from the command line using the `-P` flag:

```bash
quarto render report.qmd -P species:Gentoo -P year:2009
```

Quarto adds a new cell, tagged `injected-parameters`, right after your `parameters` cell, which assigns the new values.
Since it runs after your defaults, its values win.
Overriding parameters requires the **papermill** package to be installed in the Python environment Quarto uses; if it isn't, Quarto stops with an error asking you to install it.

To keep a set of parameter values together, you can put them in a YAML file:

```{.yaml filename="params-gentoo.yml"}
species: Gentoo
year: 2009
show_details: false
```

Then reference it when rendering:

```bash
quarto render report.qmd --execute-params params-gentoo.yml
```

You can also set parameters when rendering from Python with the `execute_params` argument to `quarto.render()`, covered in @sec-render-from-python.

::: callout-important

## Parameter values must be valid YAML

However you set them, parameters reach your document through YAML serialization.
Every value must therefore be something YAML can represent: strings, numbers, booleans, and lists or nested maps of those.
You cannot pass Python objects as parameters---a data frame, a fitted model, or a function will not survive the trip.

When a parameter needs to stand in for a complex object, pass a value that identifies it instead: a file path, a database query, or an ID that the document uses to load the object itself.

:::

You've now seen the most common things Python code cells produce: values you can weave into your text, data frames and tables, plots, and reports that vary with parameters.
In each case, the defaults give you a working document, and a few options get you closer to what you want.
The rest of this chapter collects the details behind those options, from execution options and figure formats to rendering and the Python environment Quarto runs in.

## Execution {#sec-execution-options-python}

@sec-code introduced cell-level options like `echo` and `include`.
Many of these options can also be set at the document level to apply to all code cells.

### Document-level execution options

Set execution options that apply to all cells in your document header:

```yaml
---
title: My Report
echo: false
warning: false
---
```

Common document-level execution options include the following, which take `true` or `false` unless noted otherwise:

- `eval`: Whether to execute code cells
- `echo`: Whether to display source code
- `output`: Whether to include results (can also be set to `asis`)
- `warning`: Whether to include warnings
- `error`: Whether to include errors (without halting)
- `include`: Whether to include any output at all

Additionally, `fig-width` and `fig-height` can be set at the document level to define default figure dimensions in inches.
With the Jupyter engine, these are only available at the document level, because Quarto applies them as matplotlib's defaults when the kernel starts.

Furthermore, the `jupyter` key in your document header chooses which Jupyter kernel runs your code:

```yaml
---
title: My Document
jupyter: python3
---
```

`python3` is the name of the default Python kernel, and you rarely need to set this yourself: Quarto picks a kernel based on the language of the first code cell.
Setting it is useful when you have several kernels installed, for example one per project, and want to be explicit about which one a document uses.
@sec-quarto-finds-python describes how Quarto locates Python and its kernels.

The `cache` option is also set at the document level:

```yaml
---
execute:
  cache: true
---
```

With the Jupyter engine, caching works on the whole document rather than on individual cells: if none of the code has changed since the last render, Quarto reuses the stored results instead of running any of the cells.
Caching requires the [**jupyter-cache**](https://jupyter-cache.readthedocs.io/) package.

### Cell-level execution options

Individual code cells can override document-level settings.
The Jupyter engine supports a smaller set of cell-level options than knitr.

- Some options control code appearance:
  - `code-fold`: Collapse code into an expandable section
  - `code-summary`: Text shown for collapsed code (e.g., "Show code")
  - `code-line-numbers`: Add line numbers to code

- Some control the output:
  - `output`: Whether and how to show results (`true`, `false`, or `asis` to indicate that the output is raw markdown and should not have any of Quarto's standard enclosing markdown)
  - `warning`: Whether to include warnings
  - `error`: Whether to include errors (without halting)

- Some are specific to code cells that generate figures:
  - `fig-cap`: Caption
  - `fig-alt`: Alternative text
  - `fig-align`: Alignment: `left`, `center`, or `right`
  - `out-width` and `out-height`: Output dimensions as percentage (80%), pixels (400px), or page metrics (0.5\linewidth)

- Finally, `tags` attaches Jupyter cell tags, such as the `parameters` tag from @sec-parameters-python.

For a complete list of Jupyter cell options, see the [Quarto reference](https://quarto.org/docs/reference/cells/cells-jupyter.html).

## Data frame printing {#sec-df-print-python}

Quarto's `df-print` option only applies to the knitr engine.
With Jupyter, the data frame library decides how a data frame displays: Quarto includes whatever display the library provides, picking the HTML version for HTML output and the plain-text version for other formats.

For polars, you control the display with `pl.Config`.
For example, to show more rows and widen string columns throughout a document, set them in a code cell near the top:

```{python}
#| eval: false
pl.Config.set_tbl_rows(20)
pl.Config.set_fmt_str_lengths(50)
```

To change the display for a single result only, use `pl.Config` as a context manager:

```{python}
#| eval: false
with pl.Config(tbl_rows=5):
    display(penguins)
```

## Graphics devices {#sec-graphics-devices-python}

Python doesn't have graphics devices in the sense that knitr does.
Instead, plotnine draws its plots with matplotlib, and Quarto tells matplotlib which file format to save figures in when the kernel starts.

You control this with the `fig-format` option, which works across all Quarto engines:

```yaml
---
format:
  html:
    fig-format: svg
---
```

Common choices include the following:

- The `retina` format is the default for HTML output. It creates PNG images at twice the usual resolution, so they look sharp on high-density screens.
- The `png` format creates standard-resolution PNG images.
- The `svg` format creates scalable images in vector format. Figures created this way are sharp at any zoom level.
- The `pdf` format generates figures in PDF format. It is the default for LaTeX/PDF output.

The related `fig-dpi` option sets the resolution, in dots per inch, of PNG figures.

::: callout-tip

## Automatic format selection for PDF

Because each output format has its own default `fig-format`, you get PNG figures in HTML and PDF figures in PDF output without setting anything.
That way, you don't need to set `fig-format` differently for each format.

:::

<!-- No python counterpart. -->
<!-- The R chapter discusses how `dev` and `fig-format` interact; there is no `dev` option with the Jupyter engine. -->

## Conditional execution {#sec-conditional-execution-python}

Sometimes you need code to behave differently depending on the output format.
There are no Python helper functions for this like knitr's `is_html_output()`, but Quarto exposes format information through the `QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO` environment variable, which it sets during rendering.[^python-1]
The variable holds the path to a JSON file, which you can read with the standard library:

[^python-1]: For more information, see Quarto documentation on execution context information at <https://quarto.org/docs/advanced/quarto-execute-info.html>.

```{{python}}
import json
import os

with open(os.environ["QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO"]) as f:
    info = json.load(f)

format_name = info["format"]["identifier"]["base-format"]

if format_name == "html":
    # HTML-specific code
    ...
```

Because Quarto only sets `QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO` while rendering, this code fails when you run it interactively.
If you want the cell to also work in your editor, check for the variable first with `os.environ.get("QUARTO_EXECUTE_INFO")`, and fall back to a default format when it's missing.

<!-- No python counterpart. -->
<!-- The R chapter shows `knitr::pandoc_to()` here. -->

## Interactive output {#sec-interactive-output-python}

Many Python packages produce interactive HTML output---plots, tables, maps---that Jupyter knows how to display.
Import the package and call the function as you would in a Jupyter notebook.
For example, you can use code cells that produce interactive plots with [plotly](https://plotly.com/python/):

```{python}
#| eval: false
import plotly.express as px

px.scatter(
    penguins,
    x="flipper_length_mm",
    y="body_mass_g",
    color="species",
)
```

Or interactive tables with [itables](https://mwouts.github.io/itables/):

```{python}
#| eval: false
from itables import show

show(penguins, pageLength=5)
```

Or interactive maps with [ipyleaflet](https://ipyleaflet.readthedocs.io/), one of many packages built on [Jupyter Widgets](https://ipywidgets.readthedocs.io/):

```{python}
#| eval: false
from ipyleaflet import Map, Marker

m = Map(center=(40.73, -73.99), zoom=12)
m.add(Marker(location=(40.73, -73.99), title="New York City"))
m
```

It is important to note that interactive output only works in HTML output formats.
A Jupyter output can come in several versions, such as HTML, an image, and plain text, and Quarto picks the best one the output format supports.
Most interactive packages only provide an HTML version and a plain-text description, so when you render to PDF or Word you won't see an error, but you will get a line of text like `Map(center=[40.73, -73.99], ...)` or nothing at all, rather than a plot, table, or map.

To provide something better, use the format information from @sec-conditional-execution-python to include interactive output only in HTML, falling back to a static plot or table for other formats.
For example, show an itables table in HTML and a great_tables table everywhere else, or a plotly plot in HTML and its plotnine equivalent everywhere else.

::: callout-note

## Widget dependencies and self-contained documents

Each interactive package brings its own JavaScript and CSS dependencies.
In self-contained HTML documents (`embed-resources: true`), these dependencies are bundled into the file, which can increase its size.
If your document uses many different interactive packages, consider using the default non-self-contained output and hosting the result as a directory.

:::

## Raw markdown output {#sec-raw-markdown-output-python}

Sometimes you want your Python code to produce raw markdown that Quarto processes directly, rather than being wrapped in output containers.
Use `output: asis` for this, and you will usually want `echo: false` as well:

::: {.rendered}

```{{python}}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
print("## A Dynamic Heading\n")
print("This paragraph was generated by Python.")
```

```
## A Dynamic Heading

This paragraph was generated by Python.
```

:::

One common use case is programmatically generating sections in a loop.
For example, you can iterate over the groups in a dataset, emitting a heading and some content for each:

::: {.rendered}

```{{python}}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
for (species,), group in penguins.group_by("species", maintain_order=True):
    print(f"### {species} penguins\n")
    print(f"Mean body mass: {round(group['body_mass_g'].mean())} grams.\n")
```

```
### Adelie penguins

Mean body mass: 3701 grams.

### Chinstrap penguins

Mean body mass: 3733 grams.

### Gentoo penguins

Mean body mass: 5076 grams.
```

:::

Separating each piece of output with a blank line is important: `print()` adds one newline, and the extra `\n` gives the second one, which tells Quarto to treat the heading and the paragraph as distinct markdown blocks rather than running them together.

This approach works well for text output, but not for code cells that produce figures or tables.

If you only need a piece of markdown as a cell's result, rather than a whole cell's printed output, you can also return a `Markdown` object from `IPython.display`, such as `Markdown(f"**{species}** penguins")`.
Quarto treats it as markdown even without `output: asis`.

## Rendering {#sec-python-rendering}

### Rendering from Python {#sec-render-from-python}

The [**quarto**](https://pypi.org/project/quarto/) Python package provides a function to render documents directly from Python, without using the terminal.
This package is optional---you don't need it to use Quarto with Python.
It's a convenience for scripts and pipelines written in Python, for example a script that renders a report for each species in turn.

You can use `quarto.render()` to render a document:

```python
import quarto

quarto.render("report.qmd")
quarto.render("report.qmd", output_format="pdf")
```

<!-- No python counterpart. -->
<!-- The R chapter shows `quarto_preview()` here; the quarto Python package has no preview function. Use `quarto preview` from the terminal instead. -->

You can also pass parameters directly when rendering with `quarto.render()` using the `execute_params` argument:

```python
quarto.render(
    "report.qmd",
    execute_params={"species": "Gentoo", "year": 2009},
)
```

Values passed this way are serialized to YAML before reaching your document, so the restrictions in @sec-parameters-python apply---`execute_params` takes a Python dictionary, but not arbitrary Python objects:

```python
# Fails: a data frame is not a YAML value
quarto.render("report.qmd", execute_params={"data": penguins})
```

### Rendering Python scripts {#sec-render-scripts-python}

You can render Python scripts (`.py` files) directly with Quarto, without converting them to `.qmd` files first.
This uses the *percent format*, a convention for marking cells in plain scripts that editors like Positron and VS Code also understand.

- Lines starting with `# %%` start a new code cell
- Lines starting with `# %% [markdown]` start a new markdown cell, in which every line is commented with `#`
- Lines starting with `#|` are code cell options

Here's an example script that includes both markdown and code cells:

```{.python filename="analysis.py"}
# %% [markdown]
# ---
# title: Penguin Analysis
# author: Soraya Drake
# format: html
# ---

# %% [markdown]
# ## Setup

# %%
import polars as pl
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins
from plotnine import aes, geom_point, ggplot, theme_minimal

penguins = pl.from_pandas(load_penguins())

# %% [markdown]
# ## Bill Size Analysis
#
# @fig-bill-sizes shows the relationship between
# bill length and depth.

# %%
#| label: fig-bill-sizes
#| fig-cap: Bill dimensions by species
#| warning: false
(
    ggplot(penguins, aes(x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", color="species"))
    + geom_point()
    + theme_minimal()
)
```

You can render the script just like a `.qmd` file:

```bash
quarto render analysis.py
quarto preview analysis.py
```

This lets you keep your analysis as a plain Python script that can also be run with `python analysis.py` or interactively, cell by cell, in your editor.
Quarto can also render Jupyter notebooks (`.ipynb` files) directly, in the same way.

## Environment {#sec-python-environment}

### How Quarto finds Python {#sec-quarto-finds-python}

Quarto looks for a Python installation in the following order:

1. The `QUARTO_PYTHON` environment variable, if set
2. The `python` executable found on your system `PATH`, if it belongs to a conda environment
3. The `python3` executable found on your system `PATH`

This is why activating a virtual environment, which puts that environment's Python first on your `PATH`, is usually all you need to do for Quarto to use it.

If Quarto is using a different Python than you expect, you can override the lookup by setting `QUARTO_PYTHON` to the path of your preferred Python binary.
In a Quarto project, one way to do this is an [`_environment` file](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/environment.html) alongside `_quarto.yml`:

```{.bash filename="_environment"}
QUARTO_PYTHON=/opt/venvs/penguins/bin/python
```

Quarto reads `_environment` from the project root during rendering, so this applies to every document in the project.
Use `_environment.local` for values specific to your own machine---Quarto adds `/_*.local` to `.gitignore` to keep them out of version control.
Variables already set in your shell take precedence over the file, and because this is a project-level feature, a standalone document outside a project needs `QUARTO_PYTHON` set in your environment instead.

Finding Python is only half the story.
Your code runs in a Jupyter *kernel*, and a kernel is described by a *kernelspec* that names the Python executable the kernel starts.
That executable is usually the same Python Quarto found, but it doesn't have to be: a kernelspec named `python3` installed elsewhere on your system can point to a different Python entirely.
When the Python Quarto finds lives in a virtual environment that has its own kernelspec, Quarto prefers that one, which keeps the two in step.
You can list the kernels available to a Python environment with `jupyter kernelspec list`.

To see which Python installation and kernels Quarto is currently using, run `quarto check` from the terminal:

```bash
quarto check jupyter
```

The output will include the detected Python version and path, along with the Jupyter version and the available kernels, e.g.:

```bash
Quarto 1.10.18
[✓] Checking Python 3 installation....OK
      Version: 3.12.6
      Path: /Users/mine/Desktop/posit/quarto-tdg/.venv/bin/python3
      Jupyter: 5.9.1
      Kernels: python3

[✓] Checking Jupyter engine render....OK
```

If the Python path shown doesn't match what you expect, that's likely the source of any "module not found" or version mismatch issues.
A common cause is a Terminal where the virtual environment isn't activated, or where a different one is.

### Diagnosing environment issues {#sec-diagnosing-env-python}

When Quarto renders a document, it starts a fresh Jupyter kernel.
This kernel might use a different Python installation or virtual environment than what you use interactively.
In particular, packages you've installed in one environment are not available in another, and environment variables like `PATH` may also differ.

Add a code cell to your document that outputs your session information:

```{{python}}
import sys

print(sys.version)
print(sys.executable)
sys.path
```

This will show the Python version, the path to the Python executable, and the directories Python searches for packages during rendering.
To check the version of a specific package, use `importlib.metadata`:

``` python
from importlib.metadata import version

version("polars")
```

Compare either output with your interactive Python session to identify discrepancies.
If `sys.executable` differs, that explains missing packages; see @sec-quarto-finds-python for how to control which Python installation Quarto uses.

You can watch Quarto perform the search described in @sec-quarto-finds-python by adding `--log-level debug` to `quarto check`:

```bash
quarto check jupyter --log-level debug
```

The output names each Python executable Quarto tries, in order, which one it found, and which kernel it prefers (the output below is trimmed):

```bash
Quarto version: 1.10.18
Quarto 1.10.18
Looking for Python binaries and Jupyter capabilities.
Looking for Jupyter capabilities from conda 'python' binary
[execProcess] python /Applications/quarto/share/capabilities/jupyter.py
[execProcess] Success: true, code: 0
[execProcess] python3 /Applications/quarto/share/capabilities/jupyter.py
[execProcess] Success: true, code: 0
Python found at '/Users/mine/Desktop/posit/quarto-tdg/.venv/bin/python3'
...
Preferring a venv-based python kernel at /Users/mine/Desktop/posit/quarto-tdg/.venv/share/jupyter/kernels/python3
```

This is the quickest way to tell whether a stale `QUARTO_PYTHON` or an unexpected `PATH` is redirecting Quarto to a Python installation you didn't intend.

## Multiple languages {#sec-multiple-languages-python}

While this chapter focuses on Python with the Jupyter engine, that's only one of the combinations of languages and engines Quarto supports.
Quarto runs each document through exactly one engine, and with the Jupyter engine, all of a document's code runs in a single kernel.
A document with a Python kernel therefore runs only Python: if you add a cell in another language, such as `{bash}`, Quarto doesn't execute it and shows it as plain code instead.

When a project calls for more than one language, you have several options, depending on whether the languages need to share data and whether they need to be in the same document.

- **Python and R, sharing objects.**
  Any document with an `{r}` cell uses the knitr engine, which runs Python cells through the **reticulate** package in the same session as R.
  Each language can then read the other's objects directly, as described in @sec-multiple-languages.
  Use this when one step of your analysis is easier in one language and the next step is easier in the other, for example fitting a model in Python and then plotting its predictions with ggplot2.

- **Python and R, side by side.**
  You can use the same knitr setup without passing anything between the languages, with each language doing its own work.
  This is useful when you want to show the same task in both languages, as in teaching materials or documentation for a tool with both R and Python interfaces, like plotnine and ggplot2 or great_tables and gt.
  Tabsets work well for this, letting readers pick their language:

  ````markdown
  ::: panel-tabset

  ## R

  ```{{r}}
  library(palmerpenguins)
  mean(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  ```

  ## Python

  ```{{python}}
  import polars as pl
  from palmerpenguins import load_penguins
  penguins = pl.from_pandas(load_penguins())
  penguins["body_mass_g"].mean()
  ```

  :::
  ````

  Each language loads its own copy of the data, so neither depends on the other.
  Keep in mind that the Python cells still run through reticulate, not Jupyter, so the Jupyter-specific features in this chapter, like the `parameters` tag and the `jupyter` key, don't apply.

- **Python and Observable JS.**
  `{ojs}` cells aren't run by an engine at all: Quarto passes them through to the HTML output, and they run in the reader's browser.
  They therefore work alongside Python cells in a Jupyter document.
  Use this when you want readers to interact with your results, such as filtering a table or adjusting a plot with a slider, without running a Python server.
  The two languages don't share a session; to give OJS your data, write it to a file in a Python cell and read that file in an OJS cell with `FileAttachment()`.

- **R with the Jupyter engine.**
  The Jupyter engine isn't limited to Python.
  If you install an R kernel, such as [IRkernel](https://irkernel.github.io/), and set `jupyter: ir` in your document header, your `{r}` cells run through Jupyter instead of knitr.
  Use this if you prefer working in Jupyter notebooks and want the same tools and workflow, like the `parameters` tag, for R as for Python.
  You lose knitr-specific features, like `df-print` and graphics devices.

- **Different languages in different documents.**
  Within a project, each document chooses its own engine, so one file can use knitr and R while another uses Jupyter and Python.
  This book works this way: @sec-r is rendered with knitr and this chapter with Jupyter.
  Use this when different people, or different parts of a project, work in different languages, and each part can stand on its own.
  If one document needs results from another, pass them through files, such as CSV or Parquet, written by one document and read by the other.

For the full set of rules Quarto uses to choose an engine---including what happens in documents with no Python cells at all---see @sec-engine-selection.
